lines.text: What's it going to be? Learn a new opening, drill your weaknesses, or review a game — your call.
Got it — after your move, they play Pawn to c 5 if it's still legal.
This game is the Sicilian Defense.

It's level, so make chances: one move here creates an imbalance — doubled pawns for them — and the quiet move keeps it level. The rule behind e4: stake out the center and grab space with the pawn to e4, because pieces behind a strong center reach either wing in a move or two.
Got it — after your move, they play c takes d 4 if it's still legal.

It's the Smith-Morra Gambit of the Sicilian Defense. It offers a pawn, and they almost always take it on d4. In the main line you stay a pawn down for at least 4 moves, playing for time instead of material.
Got it — after your move, they play d takes c 3 if it's still legal.
It's the Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted of the Sicilian Defense.
Got it — after your move, they play Pawn to d 6 if it's still legal.

They play d6 first, to free their bishop on c8 for bishop to d7 — a piece left at home cannot join the fight, and whoever has more pieces out wins the fights when the center opens. Knight takes c3, not b-pawn takes c3, which would leave an isolated pawn on c3. Your knight on c3 now touches eight squares, up from three on b1. A knight is worth the squares it reaches.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to c 6 if it's still legal.

The bishop bears down on d5, holding back their d-pawn, e6, holding back their e-pawn, and f7, attacking their pawn there. Their bishop is still on c8, so nothing hits your bishop on c4 yet — it doesn't need a guard; development comes first.
Got it — after your move, they play Pawn to g 6 if it's still legal.

This is the Sicilian Defense: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted, Fianchetto Defense with your bishop to c4 and their d6 thrown in. They play g6 first, to free their bishop on f8 for bishop to g7. You play knight to f3 first, so you can castle next — a king left in the middle gets caught the moment the center opens.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop to g 7 if it's still legal.

Ask it of every candidate: after it, can they take anything of yours? One knight move here answers no, whatever they reply — the next-best leaves your pawn on e5 to be taken. Before the middlegame gets going, the balance sheet: it's level — you're ahead in development: three pieces out and castled, against two pieces out; on the other side, they're up a pawn — and the two hold each other.

How do you find a plan? First the forcing scan — checks, captures, threats. Then three things: where is their weakness, which of your pieces is worst, where is your pawn break? So the plan: put a rook on the open c-file. Why that piece? A position is only as strong as its worst piece.
Got it — after your move, they play King takes f 7 if it's still legal.

Before your move, checks, captures, threats: nothing of yours could be taken, and nothing of theirs was free. Their weakness was the hole on h6 that no pawn of theirs can guard. Your worst piece was the rook on a1, with no open file yet.

Bishop takes f7 with check was a mistake. That took the pawn on f7, but the king on e8 takes back — you lose a bishop for a pawn. Here's how: end every move with a sweep: what of mine is undefended right now? Loose pieces are what make their tactics work — defend a loose piece or move it before it becomes their idea. You've walked into this before — loose piece, the sixth game now — the last one was against jkern1013 2 weeks ago.
They take back with king takes f7 — anything else, like king to f8, loses material in the line that follows.
Got it — after your move, they play King to e 8 if it's still legal.

You are down material now — the job is to make it hard: keep pieces on, since every trade makes their extra material count for more, and look for counterplay. Your knight to g5 with check eyes e6, a square no pawn of theirs can ever cover. They still have two minor pieces at home — the more they wait, the more you attack. Their pawn on e7 looks like it can chase a piece you post here, but the kick costs them a pawn. Before you post a piece, always check that kick.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to f 6 if it's still legal.

Count before you take on d6: two attackers against two defenders. Not enough — start the trades there and you come out behind. Their pawn on e7 is tied down now: you hit the pawn on d6 twice and it is guarded twice — the pawn is the guard that holds it. That is what pressure buys — a piece that cannot leave. Before you take on d6, look past the trade: your bishop on d6 would stand between their queen on d8 and your queen on d1, all on one file — a pin.
Got it — after your move, they play Queen to a 5 if it's still legal.

Your next move is not a big decision — several are about equally good, so save your time for the moves that are. Your bishop on f4 is tied to guarding the knight on g5 — but their queen on a5 is just as tied to attacking it, so the guard costs you nothing. Your rook to e1 puts the rook behind your e4 pawn — it guards it now, and owns the e-file when it opens.
Got it — after your move, they play Rook to f 8 if it's still legal.

Their rook to f8 stops your queen to f7, check. Anything else, like knight to h5, gives up about a point. Their bishop on c8 is tied down now: you hit the pawn on b7 once and it is guarded once — the bishop is the guard that holds it. Their rook on f8 and bishop on g7 now stand a knight's jump apart — that is the pattern to scan for: one square your knight can reach hits both.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to g 4 if it's still legal.

Danger — a whole piece is at stake: your bishop on f4 is the only defender of your knight on g5 — and it can be taken. Remember — removing the guard takes away the piece defending a key square, and what it protected falls. It is attacked once and nothing guards it: rook takes f4 — they win a bishop.
There is something to collect, but your bishop on f4 is loose and under fire — safety first — the material is not going anywhere. Knight to b5? Then they answer rook takes f4 — they win a bishop.
Got it — after your move, they play Queen to b 4 if it's still legal.
Careful — your bishop on f4 is attacked and nothing's defending it.

Now if they go ahead with rook takes f4 anyway, you take their queen on a5 — the grab loses them material. Your knight has a fork waiting on c7 — it would hit their king on e8 and rook on a8. Find the way there.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop to e 5 if it's still legal.
Threat met. Your bishop steps out of the attack with bishop to g3.

Not urgent yet, but see it coming — their queen on b4 pins your knight on c3 against your rook on e1. Remember — a pin freezes the piece in front: it can't move without exposing the more valuable piece behind it, so it can be piled on. If your knight moves, your rook on e1 is open to their queen.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop takes g 3 if it's still legal.
Careful — your pawn on f2 guards your king, and they hit it three times — it falls unless you cover it.
Why not queen takes b4?
Got it — after your move, they play Rook takes f 2 if it's still legal.
Queen takes b4 would not have worked: it grabs the queen on b4, but bishop takes f2 with check refutes it.

The plan changes here — now it's to win their weak pawn on g6. Here's how: plant your knight on g5, in front of it, so it can never advance; then stack your rooks and queen on its file and trade off its defenders — each one is a piece of theirs tied to it. Count it: nothing of theirs guards it — the first attacker you bring wins it. Why this one and not seizing the open c-file?
Got it — after your move, they play Queen takes b 3 if it's still legal.
That plan came before seizing the open c-file because no pawn of theirs can protect their pawn on g6, so every piece that guards it is a piece doing nothing else.

Careful — this costs a pawn if you ignore it: your pawn on b2 is the only defender of your knight on c3 — and it can be taken. It is attacked twice and nothing guards it: rook takes b2 — they win a pawn.
Why not rook takes g4?
Got it — after your move, they play Rook takes b 2 if it's still legal.
Rook takes g4 would not have worked: it grabs the knight on g4, but queen takes b2 refutes it.

That's the price of a-pawn takes b3: no pawn of yours can cover b5 again, and their knight on c6 is two moves from it; from there it would hit your knight on c3. Keeping b5 guarded is part of this structure from here.

Their rook takes b2 is imprecise. Rook to f7 was their move — the idea is to park a piece on e5, where none of your pawns can attack it. That was the move here — it takes back the queen. After the a-pawn takes b3, b5 is weak for good, and their knight on c6 gets there in two — that square is theirs now.
Got it — after your move, they play King to f 7 if it's still legal.
Careful — your rook on g6 hangs: nothing guards it, so taking it costs them nothing.

Rook takes d6? Then they answer e-pawn takes d6 — you come out behind on material, giving up a rook for a pawn. Knight to f8? Then they answer king takes f8 — they win a knight. After their king to f7, you're at a fork in the road: one move limits the damage. Take the extra minute. Of the two plans on offer, the stronger is an attack on their king; the d-file falls short by about a point.
Got it — after your move, they play Rook to f 2 if it's still legal.
Threat met. Your rook steps out of the attack with rook to g5.
Rook to g5 pays that price: your rook now guards b5.

Rook to g5 wins by force: you win a rook — it lands three moves later with king takes f2. Anything else, like rook takes d6, gives up about a point. That was the move here — it saves it from their king on f7, and from g5 it hits their knight on g4. Notice what their rook gave up by going to f2: your pawn on b3 isn't attacked any more, so the move you owed it is free again.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop to d 7 if it's still legal.

Their bishop to d7 is a mistake — it throws away more than a point of advantage. C-knight to e5 was their move — it would park a piece on e5, where none of your pawns can attack it. That gives you a way back into the game — look for it. That was the move here — it repositions the knight to d5, eyeing f4, e7 and f6 — e7 and f6 sit right beside their king. Don't park a piece on e3 — it's the first stop for your knight on d5 on the way to h4.
Got it — after your move, they play Rook takes g 2, check if it's still legal.
That's three in a row.
Careful — their bishop on d7 hits your rook on g4, and a guard does not help: the bishop is worth less than your rook.

Rook takes g4 was the only move that kept you in it. e5 didn't work: they answer c-knight takes e5 — they win a pawn. The position has turned sharp — one move here is far better than the rest, so calculate before you move.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop takes g 4 if it's still legal.
They play bishop takes g4 — they win a rook. Anything else, like rook to h8, gives up five points or more. That was the move here — it takes back the rook.
The plan here: plant the knight on the g5 outpost, where no pawn can challenge it — a piece no pawn can chase stays there for the whole game.
Got it — after your move, they play King to g 8 if it's still legal.
They are hitting your knight on h7, and nothing guards it — it is lost unless it moves or gets a guard.

Their king to g8 is a mistake — it throws away more than a point of advantage. King to g6 was their move — it would attack the knight on h7. That brings you level — look for the move that does it. Your rook to f1 with check takes the open f-file, where the rook belongs.
Got it — after your move, they play e takes f 6 if it's still legal.
The natural alternative, king to h8, fails: they play king to h8 and you answer knight takes g4 — you win a bishop. That was the move here — it checks the king on g8.
Got it — after your move, they play King to f 8 if it's still legal.
Their bishop has nothing defending it — find it, and taking it costs you nothing back. Before you take, check what taking it allows.

That was the move here — it forks the king on g8 and the bishop on g4. Their king on f8 is hiding behind your own knight on f6 — it's on your rook's f-file. Move the knight off the line and it's check. Things have got concrete — only one move really works here; find it before anything else.
Got it — after your move, they play King to e 7 if it's still legal.
That's five in a row.

That was the move here — it wins the bishop on g4. The plan changes here — now it's to get your passed pawn on g3 promoting. Here's how: it is 5 squares from queening; escort it with your king and pieces, and push it one safe square at a time — every push brings it closer to promotion. Why this one and not winning their weak pawn on d6?
Got it — after your move, they play King to f 7 if it's still legal.
That plan came before winning their weak pawn on d6 because nothing of theirs can stop your g-pawn with a pawn, so a piece of theirs must stand guard against it.

A rook-and-minor ending is won slowly: keep the pieces active and pile on the weakest pawn. Your knight to f6 lands on the f6 outpost, a square none of their pawns can attack — a piece no pawn can chase stays there for the whole game.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to d 4 if it's still legal.

Watch e3 — a knight lands there in 2 and forks your king on g2 and rook on f1, so take the square away before it arrives. Before the king moves, count the checks it walks into on each square. Your g4 pushes your passed pawn — passed pawns must be pushed. After the pawn to g4, f4 is weak for good, and their knight on d4 gets there in two — that square is theirs now.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight takes b 3 if it's still legal.

g5 makes f6 an outpost for the knight — no enemy pawn can ever challenge it. After the pawn to g5, h5 is weak for good, but their knight needs four moves to get there — an eternity, so don't worry about it.
Got it — after your move, they play King to g 7 if it's still legal.

Give your knight on d5 a second guard — it is your best piece, and one defender is one capture away from losing it. Knight to d5 with check forces the king to react, seizing the initiative for a move.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to c 5 if it's still legal.
The rook trains on the pawn on d6 — pressure they have to answer.
Got it — after your move, they play Rook to f 8 if it's still legal.

Their rook to f8 prepares knight to e6, to hit your pawn on g5. The king marches up — in the endgame it stops hiding and becomes a fighting piece. Here is what they are after: the e-file — a rook on an open file reaches your camp.
Got it — after your move, they play King takes f 8 if it's still legal.

They take back with king takes f8 — anything else, like knight takes e4, loses material in the line that follows. Watch where their moves are going — pushing their passed pawn on the a-file — every push brings it closer to promotion. A knight ending plays much like a pawn ending — king activity and the passed pawn decide it.
Got it — after your move, they play Pawn to a 5 if it's still legal.
g6 — now king to f7 doesn't work: your pawn on g6 covers f7. Their passed pawn is on a5 now — four squares from queening.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to b 3 if it's still legal.
Knight to c3 — now b5 doesn't work: the pawn would just be lost on b5. Your knight to c3 eyes d5 and b5, squares no pawn of theirs can ever cover. What's the priority here?
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to d 4, check if it's still legal.
The priority was their pawn on d6 — it's isolated — no pawn beside it can defend it.

Their knight to d4 does two jobs: it stops your knight to b5, and it prepares b5. They have given up on pushing their passed pawn on the a-file. Their plan is taking shape: pushing their passed pawn on the b-file — every push brings it closer to promotion.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to e 6, check if it's still legal.

King to g5 holds against the first replies, but after they play king to g7, you play king to f4, king takes g6 breaks it — the line had to be followed to the end. Here's how: follow every check, capture and threat until nothing is forcing, then judge the position. If they still have a capture at the end of your line, you have not finished. You've walked into this before — stopping the calculation early, the fourth game now — the last one was against Coach yesterday. King to g5 was a mistake — it cost more than a point of advantage. They answer king to g7, you play king to f4, and they play king takes g6.
Their knight to e6 with check is a mistake — it throws away more than a point of advantage. King to g7 was their move — it would win a pawn.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to f 4 if it's still legal.

The king trains on the knight on e6 — pressure they have to answer. Your king steps up to f6: with the queens off it is no longer a target but a fighting piece, and from the middle it reaches either wing.
Got it — after your move, they play King to g 8 if it's still legal.

The natural alternative, king to e8, fails: they play king to e8 and you answer g8=Q+ — you come out ahead on material. g7 with check forces the king to react, seizing the initiative for a move. Your plan from here: the a-file — a rook on an open file reaches their camp.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to h 5, check if it's still legal.

The plan changes here — now it's to win their weak pawn on d6. Here's how: plant your knight on d5, in front of it, so it can never advance; then bring your king and pieces to it and trade off its defenders — each one is a piece of theirs tied to it. Count it: you hit it once and nothing of theirs guards it. Why it matters: no pawn of theirs can protect their pawn on d6, so every piece that guards it is a piece doing nothing else.
Got it — after your move, they play Pawn to a 4 if it's still legal.
Careful — your pawn on g7 guards your king, and they hit it twice — it falls unless you cover it. Nothing guards one of their pieces — whatever takes it is not taken back.

e5? Then they answer d-pawn takes e5 — they win a pawn. That was the move here — it attacks the knight on h5. Watch where their moves are going — the g-file — a rook on an open file reaches your camp. That's two times now they've left a piece loose under your attack — they don't check what their move leaves behind. After every move of theirs, look first for what they left loose.
Got it — after your move, they play King to h 7 if it's still legal.

Their king to h7 is a blunder — they could have won your pawn on g7, and it is still hanging — see to it. King takes g7 was their move — it would win a pawn. That was the move here — it wins the knight on h5. You could take on d6 right now, but the threat is stronger than carrying it out — the material will keep, so keep it hanging over them and improve first. Pieces against bare pawns — the pawns are the only counterplay, so stop the most advanced one first; then king and pieces together finish it.
Got it — after your move, they play King takes g 8 if it's still legal.

After their king taking on g8, one move keeps the win, and only one. Worth thinking it through. A king move here makes them commit their a-pawn — a committed pawn is fixed, and becomes something to aim at. A piece for two pawns — you are a pawn up overall.
Got it — after your move, they play Pawn to d 5 if it's still legal.
That's seven in a row.

King to g6 — now king to g7 doesn't work: your king on g6 covers g7. Anything else, like king to g4, gives up five points or more. After their pawn to d5, two moves keep the win. The rest give it away. Their pawn moved from d6 to d5, so it is no longer the weak pawn you were besieging. That plan is off.
Got it — after your move, they play King to h 8 if it's still legal.
There's a forced mate here — mate in 3.
Got it — after your move, they play King to g 8 if it's still legal.
There's a forced mate here — mate in 2.
Got it — after your move, they play King to f 8 if it's still legal.
There's a mate in one here.
Checkmate — you win. That's the whole game, opening to mate. Mate: the queen on d8 checks the king on f8; e7, e8, f7, g7 and g8 are covered.
